input.brief:
INTERPRETATION: The operator wants 20 complete, spoken-English Instagram Reels/TikTok scripts (35–60 s each) for Kevin Martinez of Livetrust Financial. The client profile says the main format is carousels, but today's job asks for Reels, so I'm treating Reels as the deliverable for this job. The goal is educational content about business financing that helps people discover Kevin, keeps them watching, gets shared, and starts qualified DM conversations. We never promise virality, and views are not leads. "Recent TikTok/Instagram research" means a check of format and narrative trends that AG-002 actually verifies with real, cited sources. If AG-002 can't reach or verify a source, it must say so plainly and must not invent trends, metrics or examples. This is the first delivery and the registry is empty, so there is no repetition history yet.

OBJECTIVE: Position Kevin as a clear, trustworthy, non-salesy business-financing advisor. Success signals: retention (strong hook in the first 2–3 s, a payoff that holds attention), saves and shares (practical checklists, myth-busting, mistakes to avoid), and qualified conversations (a soft DM CTA aimed at people who are actually planning a purchase or a funding request).

AUDIENCE: U.S. aspiring and current small business owners: people buying a franchise, people buying an existing business, and owners who need growth or working capital.

SCOPE: Only business financing: SBA loans, franchise financing, acquisition financing, loan readiness and deal structure. No personal finance, credit repair, trading, crypto or get-rich content.

PILLAR MIX (20 scripts): about 5 on SBA loans explained, 5 on buying a franchise, 5 on buying an existing business, 5 on getting loan ready. Within the pillars, mix the formats: myth vs. fact, top mistakes, "what lenders look at," step-by-step process, jargon explained (DSCR, SBA 7(a), equity injection, seller note, working capital), quick scenario walkthroughs (clearly hypothetical), and Q&A.

DELIVERABLE PER SCRIPT: ID (LTF-R-2026-10-12-01 to 20), pillar, topic, target viewer, estimated runtime (35–60 s at about 140–150 spoken words per minute, so about 85–145 words), hook (0–3 s, spoken plus on-screen text), timestamped body beats with spoken lines and on-screen text, a retention device, the CTA, a visual/B-roll note, the caption ending with the exact disclaimer, 3–5 relevant hashtags, the source IDs for any factual claim, and a risk/compliance note.

CTA: Approved channel is Instagram DM only. Default: "Have questions about financing your business? Send us a DM." Variants are fine if the meaning stays the same. No links, lead magnets, "comment X" automations, booking pages, websites or handles (they are TODO).

COMPLIANCE AND RISKS (flagged before work starts):
1) Never guarantee approval, rates, terms or timelines. Avoid wording like "get approved fast," "easy money" or "guaranteed."
2) Not personalized advice. Use "in general," "many lenders," "it depends."
3) Every SBA or program figure (loan caps, fees, equity injection %, guaranty %, terms, rates) must come from a verified, preferably official, source (SBA.gov, eCFR/13 CFR, current SBA SOP 50 10), with the version or date noted, and must be described as subject to change. If a figure can't be verified, leave it out.
4) Never name or imply SBA or government endorsement. No "SBA-approved advisor" or "partnered with the SBA."
5) Never state Kevin's credentials, years of experience, deal history, lender partners, geography or results. None of these are confirmed.
6) The USD 300,000 deal-size figure is provisional and ambiguous (financing amount vs. revenue vs. purchase price). Preferably don't use it. If a script does use it, it must say which of the three it means and be flagged PROVISIONAL for operator confirmation.
7) No invented testimonials, client stories or statistics. Scenarios must be labeled hypothetical.
8) No virality promises, inside the content or in our notes to the operator.
9) Brand voice: professional, clear, educational, confident, no hype. Explain jargon in plain English.

AG-005 NOTE: The Graphic Designer isn't in today's assignment schema. Visual and B-roll direction goes inline in each script (brand colors #0B2545 / #13315C / accent #E0A526 / #F4F6F8, Inter font, high-contrast captions inside safe zones). The brand kit is still a placeholder.

WORKFLOW: AG-002 research → AG-003 topic plan (20 distinct topics) → AG-004 scripts → AG-006 QA → human operator approval. Nothing is published or sent.

assignments.AG-002:
Research two areas, only with sources you actually open and cite (URL + access date 2026-10-12). Never invent sources, trends, metrics or examples. If you can't verify something, label it UNVERIFIED or leave it out.

Don't promise reach or virality, and don't present any engagement figure without a source.

(B) A fact sheet for the four pillars, preferring official sources: SBA.gov loan program pages (7(a), 504, Express, microloans), the current SBA SOP 50 10 version and effective date, 13 CFR, the FTC Franchise Rule / FDD basics, and the SBA Franchise Directory status. Cover maximum loan amounts, guaranty percentages, equity injection rules, fee structures, typical terms, use of proceeds, seller financing rules in acquisitions, and personal guarantee requirements. For each fact give: the claim, the exact figure, the source URL, the document version/date, and confidence. Mark every program figure 'subject to change.' Flag anything that changed recently or where sources conflict.

Don't research or state anything about Kevin's credentials, partners or results. Deliver a numbered source list (S01, S02…) that AG-004 can cite.
assignments.AG-003:
Using AG-002's research, build a plan of 20 distinct Reel topics: about 5 per pillar (SBA loans explained; buying a franchise; buying an existing business; getting loan ready). The registry is empty, so make sure there are no duplicates or near-duplicates inside this batch. Each topic needs a different angle and takeaway.

For each topic give: proposed ID (LTF-R-2026-10-12-01…20), pillar, working title, target viewer (franchise buyer / acquisition buyer / owner seeking growth or working capital), format (myth vs. fact, mistakes, what lenders look at, process steps, jargon explained, hypothetical scenario, Q&A), the core takeaway in one sentence, the needed source IDs, and the intended outcome (retention, save, share, or DM conversation).

Vary the formats and hooks across the 20 so no format appears more than about 4 times. Put intent-qualifying topics (e.g. 'Planning to buy a business in the next 12 months? Know these 3 numbers') in the DM-conversation slots.

Exclude personal finance, credit repair, crypto, trading and get-rich angles. Avoid the USD 300,000 figure. If you think it's essential anywhere, flag it as PROVISIONAL and say which meaning it needs. Also prepare initial registry entries (ID, pillar, topic, format, hook type) for future weeks.
assignments.AG-004:
Write 20 complete Reels scripts in spoken English, following AG-003's plan. Each script must run 35–60 s, which is about 85–145 spoken words; state the word count and estimated runtime.

Structure for each script: ID; pillar; topic; hook (0–3 s, spoken line plus on-screen text, specific and curiosity-driven, no clickbait or hype); timestamped beats with the spoken line and on-screen text for each; at least one retention device (open loop, numbered list, myth reveal, 'the mistake most buyers make'); payoff; CTA; visual/B-roll and layout note for the designer (brand colors #0B2545, #13315C, accent #E0A526, light #F4F6F8, Inter font, captions inside safe zones); caption (2–4 short lines, educational); 3–5 relevant hashtags; source IDs for every factual claim; risk note.

Rules:
- Voice: professional, clear, confident, not salesy. Explain all jargon in plain English (SBA 7(a), DSCR, equity injection, seller note, FDD, working capital).
- Never guarantee approval, rates, terms or timelines. Use hedges like 'in general', 'many lenders', 'it depends on the lender and your situation'.
- Only use program figures that are in AG-002's verified sheet, and say 'subject to change' or 'as of [date]' on screen or in speech.
- Never claim or imply SBA or government endorsement.
- Don't mention Kevin's credentials, experience, partners, location, results or testimonials. Scenarios must be explicitly hypothetical.
- Avoid the USD 300,000 figure. If you use it, specify financing vs. revenue vs. purchase price and mark it PROVISIONAL.
- CTA: Instagram DM only. Default 'Have questions about financing your business? Send us a DM.' Light variants are allowed (e.g. 'Planning a purchase? Send us a DM'). No links, 'comment X', lead magnets, websites or handles.
- Every caption must end with this exact disclaimer: 'This content is for educational purposes only and is not financial, legal or tax advice. Loan programs, terms and eligibility are subject to change and lender approval.'
- Never promise views or virality.
assignments.AG-006:
QA all 20 scripts before they go to the human operator. Check each one and report pass/fail with specific fixes.

1) Completeness: 20 scripts, unique IDs, every required field present, runtime 35–60 s (about 85–145 words; recount).
2) Accuracy: every figure or factual claim traces to an AG-002 source ID that was actually verified; program figures are marked subject to change/dated; no unverified trend stats.
3) Compliance: no guarantees of approval, rates, terms or timelines; no personalized advice; no SBA or government endorsement implied; exact disclaimer at the end of every caption.
4) Client facts: nothing about credentials, experience, partners, geography, results, testimonials, handle or website. USD 300,000 is absent, or present with its meaning specified and flagged PROVISIONAL.
5) CTA: DM only; no links, 'comment X', lead magnets or invented services.
6) Scope: business financing only.
7) Brand voice: clear, educational, no hype; jargon explained.
8) Repetition: no duplicate topics, hooks or near-identical angles within the batch.
9) No virality or view promises anywhere, including notes to the operator.
10) Hypothetical scenarios are labeled.

Escalate any unresolved item to the operator as an open question. Confirm the package is for operator approval only: nothing is published or sent.

Based on the search results, here's what you need to know about SBA loans and down payments when buying a business:

## Down Payment Requirements

For SBA 7(a) loans, you typically need to invest about 10% of the total project cost as equity. This is lower than conventional loans that might ask 20-30%. On a $500,000 deal, 10% means you put $50k down and the 7(a) loan covers the rest, assuming no seller financing.

## Flexible Down Payment Options

The good news is that the 10% doesn't have to come entirely from your own savings—up to half of it can come from a seller's note, with a minimum of 5% coming directly from you. This can be cash, a documented gift from a family member, or retirement funds rolled over through a ROBS arrangement, with the remaining 5% covered by the seller carrying a note on standby.

## Key Requirements

There are three basic things a buyer needs to secure an SBA loan: 1) a down payment, 2) good credit, and 3) a solid resume that shows you have the skills necessary to run the business you want to buy.

## Special Cases

For existing business owners looking to grow through acquisition, the SBA 7a program offers 100% acquisition financing with no down payment required if a business owner already owns a profitable, established business and wants to acquire another business of the same type.

SBA lenders need a complete file: business and personal tax returns, financial statements, debt schedule, use of funds, ownership structure, and more. Inconsistent data—revenue on your P&L that does not match tax returns, or a debt schedule that omits a loan—raises red flags and can trigger a decline for credibility reasons.

## Cash Flow and Repayment Ability
SBA lenders look closely at your debt-to-income (DTI) and debt-service coverage ratio (DSCR), which help assess your ability to handle an additional loan. Banks and other lenders will review a business's financial statements or tax returns to assess its creditworthiness and determine if it is eligible for a loan, looking for evidence of consistent revenue, profitability, and cash flow to ensure the borrower can make timely payments.

## Loan Purpose and Business Plan
SBA lenders want to know exactly where the money is going and how it will help your business grow or stabilize, so vague or inconsistent explanations for how you'll use the funds could raise more red flags. Based on the search results, here's what the FTC Franchise Rule requires regarding the FDD:

## The 14-Day Rule

Under the FTC Franchise Rule, a franchisor must deliver the Franchise Disclosure Document to a prospective franchisee at least 14 calendar days before the franchisee signs any binding agreement or pays any money to the franchisor or an affiliate.

The clock runs in calendar days, not business days. Weekends and federal holidays count. You cannot waive this period, even if you want to accelerate the process.

## The 23 Required Items

The FDD is required by the FTC Franchise Rule (16 CFR Part 436) and contains 23 items of disclosure covering the franchisor's background, fees, investment costs, territory, obligations, litigation history, financial performance, and the franchise agreement itself.

They cover, in fixed order: the franchisor's history and litigation record, bankruptcy history, initial and ongoing fees, your estimated initial investment, obligations on both sides, territory, trademarks, financing the franchisor offers, the franchisee community, advertising funds, required suppliers and earnings claims, computer systems, and how renewal, termination, transfer, and dispute resolution work.

## Purpose of the Waiting Period

These rules ensure that buyers have enough time to carefully review the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD), evaluate financial commitments, and seek legal or financial advice before signing.

Drop the viewer into the middle of something happening — a result being shown, a product being used under realistic conditions, or a problem visibly in progress. No intro. No logo. Based on the search results, here's what I found about SOP 50 10 8.1 and the related equity injection and seller note requirements:

## Overview

SBA's new SOP 50 10 8.1 takes effect October 1, 2026, and is the biggest rewrite of the business acquisition rules in 2 years.

## Equity Injection Requirements

A minimum of 10% of total project costs is required for startups and changes of ownership. The 10% injection splits into two buckets—"Unlimited Equity Injection Sources" with no cap but a minimum of 5% of the total 10% downpayment must come from this category.

## Limited Equity Injection Sources (Including Seller Notes)

The second bucket covers Standby Debt Agreements, Seller Debt, and Non-controlling Minority Equity Investments, and these sources "may provide no more than half of the required Equity Injection."

## Seller Note Requirements

Seller standby notes may count toward equity injection only if they carry zero payments, no principal and no interest, for the entire life of the SBA loan, typically 10 years, and even under those terms, seller notes can satisfy no more than 50% of the required injection.

## Change of Ownership

Change of ownership now has its own dedicated section, Appendix 15, and if any other part of the SOP conflicts with it, Appendix 15 wins.

AG-002 RESEARCH NOTES. Access date for all sources: 2026-10-12.

== METHOD AND LIMITS (read first) ==
- I ran about 30 WebSearch queries: 20 for Task A videos, plus Task B facts and platform guidance.
- Every WebFetch attempt was refused by the proxy: sba.gov (7a, 504, microloans), ecfr.gov, ftc.gov and creators.instagram.com. So NONE of the official pages below were opened directly. Every fact comes from search-result titles and snippets, and the search tool's own summaries, so accessed_via = WebSearch for everything. Confidence is lowered accordingly.
- Before publishing, the operator or QA should open the key official URLs (S01, S03, S06, S08, S10) manually and confirm the figures.

TASK A, VIDEOS:
- Web search indexes mostly TikTok /discover/ and /tag/ pages, not individual videos. Only 9 direct video URLs came up: 6 in scope (V01–V06) and 3 adjacent, real-estate DSCR videos used as format-only references (V07–V09). I did not reach the 15–30 target.
- No direct instagram.com/reel/ URL appeared in any search.
- None of the videos could be opened. No dates, metrics, transcripts or hooks are verified beyond the caption text.
- Video IDs suggest several are 2022–2024, so they are NOT recent.
- I excluded discover/tag pages because they are not video URLs.

== (A) SHORT-FORM FORMAT GUIDANCE ==
The official platform pages could not be opened. Treat every item below as directional only, not as a performance guarantee.
- P1. Instagram's official creators blog page \"Tips for Improving Your Reach\" (https://creators.instagram.com/blog/tips-for-improving-your-reach) appeared in results, but the fetch failed. Search summaries attributed these points to it and other sources:
  - Reels must be 3 minutes or less to be eligible for recommendation.
  - Post original content. Instagram is less likely to recommend reposts or videos with visible watermarks.
  - Confidence: MEDIUM-LOW (the attribution is via a summary).
- P2. Secondary blogs (Hootsuite https://blog.hootsuite.com/instagram-algorithm/ ; OpusClip https://www.opus.pro/blog/instagram-reels-caption-subtitle-best-practices) say:
  - Watch time, likes and sends/shares are key signals, and sends matter more for reaching non-followers.
  - Captions help viewers who watch with sound off.
  - Confidence: LOW to MEDIUM (secondary sources). No engagement figures should be used.
- P3. TikTok. I didn't open an official TikTok page. Secondary sources (https://www.stackmatix.com/blog/tiktok-creative-best-practices-2026 ; https://www.teleprompter.com/blog/tiktok-3-second-rule) attribute the following to TikTok for Business guidance:
  - Introduce the core proposition in the first 3 seconds.
  - Use captions or text overlays for context.
  - Suggested ad length is 21–34 s, but that guidance is for ADS, not organic content.
  - Confidence: LOW. AG-004's brief of 35–60 s organic is a reasonable choice, but no platform source verified an ideal organic length.
- P4. Patterns I saw in the captions found (qualitative only, no performance data):
  - Openers: counter-intuitive insider-truth openers (V01, \"It’s surprisingly tough…\"), 'Reality check:' openers (V04) and expectation resets (V03, \"a longshot, but not impossible\").
  - Formats: '[Jargon] explained' titles (V07); plain-English analogy plus a worked hypothetical number example plus a numbered 'who it's for' list (V09); 'How to [outcome] with an SBA loan' (V05).
  - Endings: comment-prompting questions (V03).
- Anti-patterns to avoid:
  - \"no banks, no hoops\" (V04)
  - \"that’s all the lender needs to know to approve you\" (V09)
  - keyword comment automations (V09)
  - 'link in bio / book a call'
- Unverified claims circulating in TikTok search snippets. DO NOT reuse:
  - \"5-10% down\", \"up to $5M with 10% down and 10 year term\", \"15 to 20% down… prime plus 2%\"
  - \"home equity loans… tax-deductible, easy to qualify\"
  - \"SBA loans… easy to qualify for\"
  - The SBA closing time of \"about 60 days\"

== (B) FACT SHEET ==
Every figure here is subject to change.

KEY CHANGE ALERT:
- Search results from several secondary sources (S11, S12, S13) say SBA SOP 50 10 8.1 took effect on 2026-10-01 and replaced SOP 50 10 8 (in effect since 2025-06-01).
- I couldn't open the official SBA SOP page to confirm the 8.1 text. Cite figures as \"per SBA SOP 50 10 8.1, effective Oct 1, 2026 (subject to change)\" only after the operator confirms.
- FY2027 7(a) fees took effect on 2026-10-01. Don't use FY2026 fee figures.

F1. SBA 7(a) maximum loan amounts (S03, sba.gov lender page \"Types of 7(a) loans\", per snippet):
- Standard 7(a) $5,000,000
- 7(a) Small $350,000
- SBA Express $500,000
- Export Express $500,000
- CAPLines $5,000,000
- International Trade $5,000,000
- EWCP $5,000,000
- Confidence: MEDIUM.

F2. 7(a) guaranty (S03/S04 sba.gov, S05 CRS R41146): generally up to 85% for loans of $150,000 or less, and 75% above $150,000.
- SBA Express guaranty is 50% (per the search summary; the exact sba.gov attribution is unclear).
- International Trade can get up to 90%.
- Confidence: MEDIUM.
- One snippet mentioned past TEMPORARY Express changes ($1M cap, 75% guaranty). Those are historical. Don't use them.

F3. FY2027 7(a) upfront guaranty fee (S01 SBA Information Notice 5000-881797, \"7(a) Fees Effective October 1, 2026 for Fiscal Year 2027\", published Sept 3, 2026, applies to loans approved Oct 1, 2026 to Sept 30, 2027; also S02 NAGGL). For loans over 12 months:
- $150,000 or less: 2% of the guaranteed portion
- $150,001–$700,000: 3%
- $700,001–$5M: 3.5% on the guaranteed portion up to $1M, plus 3.75% above $1M
- Lender annual service fee: 0.55% of the outstanding guaranteed balance. The FY2026 notice says this cannot be charged to the borrower.
- Some rural, manufacturing and food-supply-chain loans get 0% treatment (details not verified).
- Confidence: MEDIUM. Fees change every fiscal year.
- Recommendation: if a script mentions fees at all, describe them qualitatively (\"SBA charges a guaranty fee that varies by loan size and fiscal year\").

F4. Equity injection, startups and changes of ownership (S13 searchfunder / pioneercapitaladvisory on 8.1; S14 starfieldsmith; S18 whitefordlaw on 50 10 8):
- Minimum 10% of total project costs.
- Seller debt on FULL standby can cover no more than half of the required injection, i.e. at least 5% must come from 'unlimited' sources like cash.
- To count, a standby seller note must have NO principal or interest payments for the whole term of the SBA loan.
- Per S13, 8.1 keeps the 10% and half-max structure.
- Confidence: MEDIUM. This came from several consistent secondary sources; I didn't open the SOP itself.
- Wording for scripts: \"generally at least 10% of total project costs under current SBA rules (subject to change).\" Don't say \"10% down guaranteed.\"

F5. Changes under SOP 8.1 (secondary only, LOW-MEDIUM; S11 doeren, S12 sundancefg / jakenfinancegroup). Reported changes:
- Repayment analysis now includes the 2 most recent months of bank statements.
- Change-of-ownership loans no longer use the 7(a) Small Loan path (full underwriting instead).
- A Quality of Earnings report is required for first-time acquisitions or expansions with a purchase price of $3M or more (excluding real estate).
- Change of ownership now sits in Appendix 15.
- Recommendation: AVOID specific 8.1 details until the operator verifies them.

F6. Personal guaranty (S16 security-banks, S18 whitefordlaw; SOP 50 10 8):
- Owners with 20% or more must give a full, unconditional guaranty.
- Anyone who owned 20% or more in the prior 6 months still has to guarantee unless they fully divested.
- Confidence: MEDIUM. I couldn't confirm whether 8.1 changed this.

F7. Ownership and citizenship (S08 SBA Procedural Notice 5000-876626, dated Feb 11, 2026, effective March 1, 2026; S09 GAO B-338157; S10 SBA Policy Notice 5000-876441):
- For 7(a) and 504, 100% of direct and indirect owners must be U.S. citizens or U.S. nationals whose principal residence is in the U.S.
- Lawful permanent residents are no longer eligible owners.
- Confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH (official URL titles plus several consistent sources).
- SENSITIVE. A recent change, and it may be legally contested (the GAO opinion exists). If used, phrase it as \"check current eligibility rules with a lender.\"

F8. SBA Franchise Directory (S15 Taft law bulletin; S17 JD Supra; S16):
- The directory was reinstated with SOP 50 10 8, effective June 1, 2025.
- Per S16, franchisors had to certify by June 30, 2026. Brands that didn't were removed, and their franchisees aren't currently SBA-eligible.
- Confidence: MEDIUM for the reinstatement, LOW-MEDIUM for the certification deadline.
- Script-safe: \"For an SBA loan, lenders generally check whether the franchise brand is on SBA's Franchise Directory.\"

F9. 504 program (S06 sba.gov/loans/504-loans, per snippet): maximum $5.5 million.
- UNVERIFIED nuance: I believe $5.5M applies to certain manufacturing or energy projects, with $5M as the standard cap. Not confirmed.
- Recommendation: omit the figure, or say \"504 loans are for major fixed assets like real estate and equipment.\" Uses and terms were not verified in this session.

F10. Microloans: $50,000 or less (per search summary; the exact source URL is unclear).
- One snippet said they must be repaid within six years. CONFLICT/UNVERIFIED: I couldn't confirm the current maximum term. Omit the term.

F11. FTC Franchise Rule (16 CFR Part 436). No ftc.gov or ecfr page could be opened. From secondary sources (https://nextchapterfranchiseadvisors.com/blog/understanding-the-fdd-what-the-ftc-requires ; https://franchiseinspect.com/glossary/14-day-rule ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franchise_rule):
- The franchisor must give the FDD at least 14 calendar days before the buyer signs a binding agreement or pays money.
- The FDD has 23 items (including fees, estimated initial investment, financing offered, financial performance representations, and franchisee and outlet information).
- Confidence: MEDIUM (long-standing rule, secondary sources only).

NOT VERIFIED, so leave out of scripts:
- 7(a) maximum interest rates
- maturity terms (the common '10 yrs business / 25 yrs real estate' figure was not verified)
- detailed use-of-proceeds lists
- 504 terms and structure
- the Express turnaround time
- credit score minimums (one lender blog cited 650+; not official)
- the 100%-financing rule for same-industry expansion acquisitions (secondary only, and it may have changed under 8.1)

## Effective Date

The changes in the revised SOP 50 10 8.1 will be effective for loans receiving SBA loan numbers on or after October 1, 2026. Loans receiving an SBA loan number on or before September 30, remain subject to the requirements in SOP 50 10 8.

## Important Update History

This new version of the SOP supersedes the version of SOP 50 10 8.1 that SBA published on August 14, 2026 but never took effect. The September 25 technical-update notice supersedes the previously published, not-yet-effective 8.1 text.

## Key Changes

The updated SOP includes several significant policy changes for 7(a) lending:

- Debt Service Coverage increases for most change-of-ownership acquisitions from 1.15 to 1.25x
- A Quality of Earnings requirement for larger acquisitions, and specific timing rules for PLP processing
- Changes to financial statement requirements from 120 days to 90 days for every owner of 20% or more and each proposed guarantor

Based on the search results, here's what SOP 50 10 8.1 specifies regarding business valuation thresholds, quality of earnings, and change of ownership:

## Key Changes in SOP 50 10 8.1

**Quality of Earnings Requirement:**
For Initial Acquisition and Business Expansion transactions where the business purchase price is $3 million or more, a quality of earnings report is now required. The threshold is measured before the equity injection and before any seller note, and excludes owner-occupied real estate.

**Business Valuation - The $250,000 Threshold Eliminated:**
Under the prior SOP a lender could perform its own business valuation where the financed business value, net of real estate and equipment, was $250,000 or less. That exception does not appear anywhere in SOP 50 10 8.1, which means every change of ownership requires an independent Qualified Source valuation commissioned by and prepared for the lender.

The SOP names the qualifying credentials: Accredited Senior Appraiser (ASA), Certified Business Appraiser (CBA), Accredited in Business Valuation (ABV), Certified Valuation Analyst (CVA) and Business Certified Appraiser (BCA).

**Exemptions:**
Owner Buyout, ESOP, and cooperative transactions are exempt from the QoE mandate even at the same dollar level.

SOP 50 10 8.1 is effective October 1, 2026.

## Maximum Loan Amount and Guaranty Percentages

Most 7(a) loans have a maximum loan amount of $5 million. For most 7(a) loan programs, SBA guarantees up to 85% of loans of $150,000 or less, and up to 75% of loans above $150,000.

## SBA's Maximum Exposure

It's important to note that SBA's maximum exposure (i.e., dollars guaranteed) is $3.75 million. This means that while the loan itself can be up to $5 million, the SBA's guarantee portion is capped at $3.75 million for most 7(a) loans.

## Loan Program Variations

The guaranty percentage and maximum loan amounts can vary depending on the specific type of 7(a) loan. For example:
- 7(a) loans made under the SBA Express and Export Express delivery methods have maximum loan amounts of $500,000.
- 7(a) International Trade loans may receive a maximum guaranty of 90% or $4.5 million.

## Key Restrictions

504 loans cannot be used for working capital or inventory. This is a fundamental restriction on how the funds can be used.

## Loan Structure

504 loans involve a loan from a private sector lender with a senior lien covering up to 50% of the project cost, a loan from a CDC backed by a 100% SBA-guaranteed debenture with a junior lien covering up to 40% of the total cost, and a contribution from the borrower of at least 10% equity of the total project cost. This matches the 50/40/10 breakdown you mentioned.

## Eligible Uses

The 504 loan program provides long-term, fixed rate financing for major fixed assets that promote business growth and job creation. CDCs work with SBA and private-sector lenders to provide growing businesses with long-term, fixed-rate financing for major fixed assets, such as land, buildings, machinery, and equipment.

The search results confirm that 504 loans are specifically designed for fixed assets and explicitly prohibit use for working capital and inventory, while following the 50% lender, 40% CDC, and 10% borrower equity structure you referenced.

Based on the search results, here's information about the 7(a) loan program's terms, conditions, and eligibility:

## Terms and Maturity

For 7(a) loans, the term will be the shortest appropriate term based on the borrower's ability to repay, typically 10 years or less unless it finances or refinances real estate or equipment with a useful life exceeding 10 years, with a maximum of 25 years including extensions. A portion of a loan used to acquire or improve real property may have a term of 25 years plus an additional period needed to complete the construction or improvements.

## Use of Loan Proceeds

7(a) loans can be used for acquiring, refinancing, or improving real estate and/or buildings; short- and long-term working capital; refinancing current business debt; purchasing and installation of machinery and equipment; purchasing furniture, fixtures, and supplies; changes of ownership (complete or partial); and multiple purpose loans including any of the above.

## Eligibility Requirements

To be eligible for 7(a) loan assistance, businesses must be an operating business, operate for profit, be located in the U.S., be small under SBA Size Requirements, not be a type of ineligible business, not be able to obtain the desired credit on reasonable terms from non-Federal, non-State, and non-local government sources, and be creditworthy and demonstrate a reasonable ability to repay the loan.

## Loan Size

The maximum loan size for 7(a) loans is up to $5 million.

## Overview

On May 18, 2026, SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler announced a new rule that allows eligible borrowers to combine their 7(a) and 504 loans for up to $10 million in SBA-backed financing, increasing the cumulative loan limit from its current $5 million.

The SBA Franchise Directory contains all franchises and other brands eligible for SBA financial assistance, and only includes business models that are reviewed and found eligible by SBA. ## Personal Guaranty Requirement

The full, unlimited personal guaranty applies to anyone with 20% or more direct or indirect ownership (spouses and minor children are combined). Own 20% or more and you are an owner who has to sign a full, unlimited personal guaranty.

## Non-Controlling Minority Equity Investors

Under SBA SOP 50 10 8.1, a Non-controlling Minority Equity Investor is defined as an investor holding less than 20% of the equity, aggregated across direct and indirect ownership, who exerts no control over the operating business.

## Key Distinction

The 20% ownership threshold is the critical dividing line. To qualify as a passive investor, an investor must own less than 20% and exert no control over the operating business. Those meeting this definition as non-controlling minority equity investors may be eligible equity sources without requiring a personal guaranty, unlike owners at 20% or above.

The search results show that SOP 50 10 8.1 (effective October 1, 2026) maintains this 20% threshold as the trigger for requiring full, unlimited personal guaranties from owners.

Based on the search results, I found comprehensive information about the SBA SOP 50 10 8 and 8.1 debt service coverage requirements you're asking about:

## Debt Service Coverage Changes

Under SOP 50 10 8, lenders underwrote acquisition loans to a 1.15x minimum debt service coverage ratio, and could lean on projections to get there.

SOP 50 10 8.1 raises the floor to 1.25x for Initial Acquisitions, Owner Buyouts, and ESOP deals, keeps 1.15x only for Business Expansions, and closes the projection route entirely: coverage must be met using the last fiscal year-end or an average of the last two, on a historical or adjusted basis.

## Change of Ownership Requirements

For change of ownership transactions specifically: SOP 50 10 8.1 will also increase the debt-service coverage requirement for most change of ownership transactions from 1.15x to 1.25x. As a result, projections generally will not be able to make up for a shortfall in historical cash flow.

## Section 7(a) Loan Implications

Under the old SOP, a first-time buyer could clear a 1.15x debt service coverage test using projections. However, the debt service coverage floor rises to 1.25x for first-time acquisitions, and projections no longer count toward it.

SOP 50 10 8.1 takes effect October 1, 2026.

## SBSS Score 165 Requirement (Through March 2026)

The minimum score to pass the pre-screen for 7(a) small loans was 165 as of January 2026. In June 2025, the SBA raised the minimum SBSS score to 165, up from 155.

## Major Change: Sunset of SBSS Requirement (March 1, 2026)

However, a significant change occurred in 2026. For 7(a) loans of $350,000 or less, the SBA used to require a minimum FICO SBSS business credit score, most recently 165. That requirement ended for new loans on March 1, 2026 under SBA Procedural Notice 5000-875701.

As of March 1, 2026, the SBA eliminated the mandatory FICO SBSS score prescreen for 7(a) Small Loans of $350,000 or less, replacing the single national cutoff (most recently 165) with lender-specific credit models and a new 1.1x minimum debt service coverage ratio.

## Current Status (Post-March 2026)

Although the SBA will no longer require this score be used in this way as of March 1, 2026, it's expected that many lenders will continue using it as they've done in the past.

In summary: The 165 SBSS score was the required minimum through February 2026, but the SBA eliminated this mandatory requirement as of March 1, 2026, allowing lenders to develop their own credit assessment models instead.

## PLP Delegated Authority Overview

The Preferred Lenders Program (PLP) designates the most experienced lenders to process, close, service, and liquidate most SBA guaranteed loans without prior SBA review. claims.correct_wording: Under the FTC Franchise Rule (16 CFR Part 436), franchisors must give prospective franchisees a disclosure document. Its 23 items are listed in 16 CFR 436.5.

claims.claim: Item 7 = estimated initial investment; Item 5 = initial fees
claims.correct_wording: Item 5 discloses initial fees, meaning payments to the franchisor or its affiliates before opening. Item 7 discloses the estimated initial investment in a table.

claims.claim: Item 7 includes additional funds/working capital for an initial period
claims.correct_wording: Item 7 includes, where applicable, an 'Additional funds' line for an initial period of operation. It also covers fees, real property, equipment, leasehold improvements, opening inventory, deposits and licenses.

claims.claim: Item 19 financial performance representations, optional
claims.correct_wording: Item 19 covers financial performance representations. Franchisors do not have to make them, but if they do, the figures must have a reasonable basis and written substantiation and must appear in Item 19.

claims.claim: Current status and role of SBA Franchise Directory
claims.correct_wording: The SBA Franchise Directory is active. SOP 50 10 8 reinstated it on June 1, 2025, and SBA updates it weekly (latest version dated Oct. 9, 2026). Lenders use it to confirm that a franchise brand is eligible for SBA financing.

claims.claim: Brand eligibility does not equal borrower approval
claims.correct_wording: A brand's listing only means it is eligible. SBA says listing 'is not an endorsement or approval of the brand and does not ensure the success of the business.' Each borrower is still underwritten individually.

claims.claim: No failure/default statistics
claims.correct_wording: No failure or default statistics were researched or verified. Do not include any.

claims.claim: Working capital can be included in franchise/7(a) financing
claims.correct_wording: Working capital is an eligible 7(a) use and can be part of a franchise start-up financing request, subject to lender underwriting.

claims.claim: Scenario numbers labeled hypothetical
claims.correct_wording: Label all figures on screen: 'Hypothetical round numbers for illustration only. Not typical costs.'

claims.claim: FDD Item 7 includes 'additional funds'
claims.correct_wording: FDD Item 7 includes an 'Additional funds' estimate for an initial period of operation (16 CFR 436.5).

claims.claim: Equity injection required for start-ups including new franchises; percentage
claims.correct_wording: Under SOP 50 10 8 (June 1, 2025), the minimum equity injection for start-ups was 10% of total project costs. SOP 50 10 8.1 (Oct. 1, 2026) keeps a 10% minimum for changes of ownership. For start-ups under 8.1, I could not confirm the figure from primary text, so say 'SBA requires an equity injection for start-ups, and lenders may require more.' Check against the SOP before giving 10%.

claims.claim: Owner-operator vs absentee ownership considered
claims.correct_wording: Not verified as an SBA rule. 13 CFR 120.150 lists 'experience and depth of management' as a factor. Safe wording: 'Lenders consider who will manage the business day to day.'

claims.claim: FDD Item 7 as source for total investment
claims.correct_wording: FDD Item 7 gives the franchisor's estimated initial investment range.

claims.claim: Definition of seller note
claims.correct_wording: A seller note is a loan from the seller to the buyer for part of the purchase price. The buyer pays it back to the seller over time instead of paying that amount at closing.

claims.claim: SOP rules on seller notes counting toward equity injection and standby
claims.correct_wording: SOP 50 10 8.1 (loans numbered on or after Oct. 1, 2026): a seller note can count toward the 10% minimum equity injection only if it is on full standby, meaning no principal or interest payments, for the life of the SBA loan. Seller notes, other standby debt and minority investor equity together can cover no more than half of the required injection. This comes from law-firm and consultant summaries; check it against Appendix 15 of the SOP before publishing.

claims.claim: Do not imply 100% seller financing possible in SBA deals
claims.correct_wording: Seller notes can cover at most half of the required equity injection, so the buyer must bring at least half of it from other eligible sources. Never imply that an SBA deal can be 100% seller-financed.

claims.claim: Consideration of management experience, character, credit; credit elsewhere
claims.correct_wording: SBA's lending criteria (13 CFR 120.150) include character, reputation and credit history; experience and depth of management; and repayment ability. Separately, the business must be unable to get the credit on reasonable terms from non-government sources. That is the 'credit elsewhere' test listed on SBA.gov's 7(a) eligibility page. Its regulation section was not checked.

claims.claim: Personal guaranty for owners at or above a threshold
claims.correct_wording: Under current SOP 50 10 (8 and 8.1, as of Oct. 2026), owners of 20% or more generally must give a full, unlimited personal guaranty. Lenders can require guaranties from others. This is from lender and secondary sources; check it against the SOP.

claims.claim: Avoid 'no banks, no hoops' language
claims.correct_wording: Use only the 'Reality check' opener structure; do not copy V01 wording.

claims.claim: Definition of DSCR
claims.correct_wording: Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) = cash flow available for debt service ÷ total annual debt payments (principal plus interest). For example, 1.25x means $1.25 of cash flow for every $1.00 of debt payments.

claims.claim: Minimum DSCR under current SOP
claims.correct_wording: Under SOP 50 10 8.1 (from Oct. 1, 2026), most change-of-ownership loans (initial acquisitions, owner buyouts) reportedly need at least 1.25x, measured on historical cash flow. Business expansions stay at 1.15x. Under SOP 50 10 8 the general minimum was 1.15x. Many lenders set higher thresholds. These figures are from a law firm and secondary sources; check them against the SOP. Safe wording: 'SBA sets a minimum DSCR and many lenders require more.'

claims.claim: Correct arithmetic in hypothetical
claims.correct_wording: Example (hypothetical): $150,000 cash flow ÷ $120,000 annual debt payments = 1.25x. Label it hypothetical and recheck any figures the copywriter changes.

claims.claim: No real-estate DSCR loan concepts
claims.correct_wording: Talk only about business cash flow coverage. Leave out investor-property 'DSCR loans.'

claims.claim: Independent business valuation threshold on change of ownership
claims.correct_wording: Under SOP 50 10 8, an independent valuation was required when the amount financed minus appraised real estate and equipment exceeded $250,000, or when buyer and seller had a close relationship. Secondary sources say SOP 50 10 8.1 (Oct. 1, 2026) drops the $250,000 exception, so every change of ownership needs an independent qualified valuation. A quality of earnings report is also required for initial acquisitions and expansions with a purchase price of $3M or more. Check against the SOP before stating thresholds.

claims.claim: Verified financials (tax returns) vs seller add-backs
claims.correct_wording: Lenders check seller financials against IRS tax transcripts. Seller add-backs must be documented and may be adjusted or rejected. Under SOP 50 10 8.1, larger acquisitions need a quality of earnings review.

claims.claim: Treatment of goodwill
claims.correct_wording: Goodwill and intangible value in an SBA acquisition must be supported by the business valuation. The SBA loan for a change of ownership is reportedly capped at the valuation amount. This is a secondary source; check against the SOP.

claims.claim: Equity injection for change of ownership
claims.correct_wording: Under SOP 50 10 8.1 (Oct. 1, 2026), as under SOP 50 10 8 (June 1, 2025), complete changes of ownership require an equity injection of at least 10% of total project costs. Lenders may require more. This is from law-firm and consultant sources; check it against the SOP.

claims.claim: Lenders verify cash flow with tax returns and financial statements
claims.correct_wording: Lenders review business tax returns and financial statements and check them against IRS transcripts. Typically this covers the most recent three years.

claims.claim: Some lenders selective about smaller acquisition loans
claims.correct_wording: Not verified. Drop this point.

claims.claim: Common 7(a) documents: Form 1919, Form 413, tax returns, years
claims.correct_wording: Common 7(a) application items include SBA Form 1919 (Borrower Information Form), SBA Form 413 (Personal Financial Statement), and business and personal tax returns, generally the last three years, checked through IRS transcripts. Lenders may ask for more.

claims.claim: Lenders may request additional items
claims.correct_wording: Lenders apply their own credit procedures and may request documents beyond SBA's forms.

claims.claim: Form numbers and names still active
claims.correct_wording: Both forms appear on SBA.gov under these names: Form 1919, current version effective March 19, 2025, and Form 413, effective Feb. 13, 2025. Revisions after the 2026 citizenship changes are possible, so recheck the dates before publishing.

claims.claim: Equity injection definition and minimum for start-ups and changes of ownership
claims.correct_wording: An equity injection is the borrower's own contribution toward total project costs. The minimum is 10% for complete changes of ownership under SOP 50 10 8.1 (Oct. 1, 2026), and was 10% for start-ups and changes of ownership under SOP 50 10 8 (June 1, 2025). The start-up figure under 8.1 still needs checking against the SOP.

claims.claim: Acceptable sources: cash, documented gifts, seller notes on standby
claims.correct_wording: Sources cited by lending consultants: cash or personal savings, documented gifts (not to be repaid), and seller notes on full standby, capped at half of the required injection together with other standby debt and minority investor equity. These are not confirmed from primary SOP text; check against Appendix 15 before listing them.

claims.claim: Documentation for verifying source of injection
claims.correct_wording: Lenders must verify that the injection was made and where it came from. Typical evidence includes bank statements, copies of checks or wires, settlement statements and gift letters. Required statement periods vary by lender.

claims.claim: Avoid personal finance advice
claims.correct_wording: Describe the rules only; do not advise on how to raise the cash.

claims.claim: Underwriting considers repayment from cash flow plus credit
claims.correct_wording: SBA requires lenders to consider both credit history and the ability to repay from business earnings and cash flow (13 CFR 120.150).

claims.claim: Business plans or projections required for start-ups and acquisitions
claims.correct_wording: SBA criteria include 'projected cash flow and future prospects,' and lenders commonly ask start-ups for projections or a business plan. For acquisitions under SOP 50 10 8.1, historical cash flow carries the most weight, and projections reportedly cannot cover a shortfall.

claims.claim: FICO SBSS scores
claims.correct_wording: Leave SBSS out of the script. SBA sunset the SBSS score requirement for 7(a) Small Loans of $350,000 or less in 2026 (PN 5000-875701; supplemental guidance effective March 1, 2026).

claims.claim: Tax returns required; discrepancies need explanation; IRS Form 4506-C
claims.correct_wording: Lenders check applicants' financial data against IRS tax transcripts, generally through IRS Form 4506-C, and discrepancies must be resolved. Consultants say Form 8821 may also be accepted under SOP 50 10 8.1. Check the details against the SOP.

claims.claim: Source-of-funds documentation for equity injection
claims.correct_wording: Lenders must document where the equity injection came from and that it was put into the business, using bank statements, transfer records and similar evidence.

claims.claim: General patterns, not statistics
claims.correct_wording: No statistics were verified. Present these as general patterns only.

claims.claim: Lenders differ in appetite; delegated authority (PLP) varies
claims.correct_wording: SBA gives delegated authority (PLP) only to qualified lenders, so not every SBA lender can approve loans without prior SBA review. Lenders also set their own credit policies within SBA rules. Suggested wording: 'Lenders differ in the loan sizes, industries and deal types they focus on.' Phrase this as general guidance, not a statistic.

claims.claim: Smaller SBA acquisition loans harder to place
claims.correct_wording: Not verified. Drop it, or reframe neutrally: 'Each lender decides which deal sizes fit its business.'

claims.claim: No implied lender partnerships for Livetrust
claims.correct_wording: Do not say or imply that Livetrust has any lender partnerships or relationships. None are confirmed.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: SBA loans explained] Myth vs. fact: 'The SBA lends you the money.' In fact, participating lenders make 7(a) loans and the SBA guarantees part of them.
scripts.audience: First-time franchise and acquisition buyers who are just starting to research SBA loans
scripts.problem: Many people think the SBA itself hands out the money. So they look for the wrong door and misread who decides on approval.
scripts.amount_context: Amounts mentioned are SBA 7(a) guaranty thresholds (one hundred fifty thousand dollars loan size), not Kevin's deal size. The provisional USD 300,000 figure is not used.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "Here's a common myth: the SBA lends you the money. For seven-A loans, it doesn't." | On-screen: "MYTH: The SBA lends you the money"
scripts.script:
Here's a common myth: the SBA lends you the money. For seven-A loans, it doesn't. So who actually does?

With the SBA seven-A program, the loan comes from a participating private lender, like a bank, a credit union, or another SBA lender. The SBA guarantees part of that loan. It doesn't hand you the cash.

For most seven-A loans, that guaranty is up to eighty-five percent on loans of one hundred fifty thousand dollars or less, and up to seventy-five percent above that. Those figures are as of October twenty twenty-six and can change.

So who decides? The lender evaluates and approves the loan under SBA rules. That means your first real conversation is with a lender, and your file has to make sense to them.

Know someone researching SBA loans? Share this with them.
scripts.cta: Know someone researching SBA loans? Share this with them.

Ritmo tranquilo en las cifras, pronunciándolas despacio. Gesto de mano abierta al preguntar "So who decides?". Sonrisa leve en el CTA. Palabras totales: 133 (aprox. 55 s).

Se evita a propósito la expresión "backed by the government" y se reemplaza por el encuadre correcto: el prestamista otorga el préstamo y la SBA garantiza una parte. No se sugiere ningún respaldo de la SBA a Livetrust.

SBA guarantees up to 85% of most 7(a) loans of $150,000 or less and up to 75% above $150,000 (SBA.gov, as of Oct. 2026, subject to change).
The lender evaluates and approves the loan under SBA rules.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: SBA loans explained] Jargon explained: 'What is an SBA 7(a) loan?' A plain-English answer covering what it is and what it is commonly used for.
scripts.audience: Owners who need growth or working capital, plus would-be buyers who keep hearing '7(a)'
scripts.problem: People hear '7(a)' everywhere but can't explain it, so they can't tell whether it fits their goal.
scripts.amount_context: Five million dollars is the SBA 7(a) maximum loan amount (program cap, as of Oct. 2026), not Kevin's deal size. The provisional USD 300,000 figure is not used.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "What is an SBA seven-A loan? Here's the plain-English version." | On-screen: "SBA 7(a), explained in plain English"
scripts.script:
What is an SBA seven-A loan? Here's the plain-English version.

Seven-A is the SBA's primary loan guarantee program. A participating lender makes the loan, and the SBA guarantees part of it.

What can it pay for? Three big buckets.

One: buying a business, whether it's a complete or partial change of ownership.

Two: working capital, short or long term.

Three: hard assets, like equipment, furniture and fixtures, or real estate. It can also refinance certain current business debt.

How big? Most seven-A loans are capped at five million dollars, as of October twenty twenty-six, and that's subject to change.

Among other requirements, the business generally has to be operating, for-profit, located in the U.S., small under SBA size standards, and able to repay.

Save this so you have the definition handy.
scripts.cta: Save this so you have the definition handy.
scripts.structure: practical_explainer
scripts.recording_notes_es: Plano medio, energía calmada y didáctica, como explicando en una pizarra. Mirada a cámara todo el tiempo. Marcar "One", "Two", "Three" con los dedos y hacer una pausa corta entre cada punto. Ir un poco más despacio al decir la cifra de cinco millones y "subject to change". Cerrar con un gesto amable. Palabras totales: 127 (aprox. 52 s).
scripts.adaptation_note_es: De V03 solo se toma el formato de título "[término] explicado". El contenido de V03 trata de préstamos DSCR para inversión inmobiliaria, que están fuera de nuestro alcance, y no se usa nada de él. El guion es original y se basa solo en fuentes de la SBA.

fact_refs.claim: 7(a) is SBA's primary loan guarantee program; participating lenders make the loans and SBA partially guarantees them.

Eligible uses include complete or partial changes of ownership, short- and long-term working capital, machinery and equipment, furniture, fixtures and supplies, real estate, and refinancing current business debt.
Most 7(a) loans have a maximum of $5 million (SBA.gov, as of Oct. 2026, subject to change).
The business generally must be operating, for-profit, located in the U.S., small under SBA size standards, and creditworthy with the ability to repay, among other requirements.

scripts.why_selected_es: Es la única pieza que define el 7(a). Como referencia práctica y compacta, invita a guardarla. Además le da a la audiencia el vocabulario base para entender el resto del contenido.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: SBA loans explained] 7(a) vs. 504: which SBA program fits which purpose? (Flexible uses vs. major fixed assets.)
scripts.audience: Owners seeking growth capital, for example to buy a building, buy equipment or expand
scripts.problem: Owners assume 'an SBA loan' is a single product and don't realize the program depends on what the money is for.
scripts.amount_context: Percentages describe the typical 504 project structure (share of project cost). No dollar amounts are used, and the provisional USD 300,000 figure is not used.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "Buying a building and covering payroll are two very different needs, and the SBA has different programs for them." | On-screen: "SBA 7(a) vs. 504: which one fits?"
scripts.script:
Buying a building and covering payroll are two very different needs. And the SBA has different programs for them. Here's the quick comparison.

SBA five-oh-four is built for major fixed assets: land, buildings, machinery and equipment. It's long-term, fixed-rate financing delivered through a Certified Development Company, called a CDC, working with a private lender.

A typical structure: the lender covers up to fifty percent of the project cost, the CDC up to forty percent, and you contribute at least ten percent. Some projects need more.

One key limit: five-oh-four can't be used for working capital or inventory.

That's where seven-A comes in. It's more flexible: working capital, buying a business, equipment, real estate, and refinancing certain business debt.

Figures are as of October twenty twenty-six and subject to change. Which one fits depends on your situation. Save this.
scripts.cta: Save this.

scripts.recording_notes_es: Plano medio. Para la comparación, mover levemente el cuerpo o la mano hacia un lado al hablar del 504 y hacia el otro al hablar del 7(a). Tono seguro y pausado. Pausa marcada antes de "One key limit" para destacar la restricción. Contar los porcentajes despacio. Mirada a cámara en el cierre. Palabras totales: 144 (aprox. 59 s).
scripts.adaptation_note_es: Guion original, sin referencia externa. El mecanismo es una comparación por propósito de uso (activo fijo vs. usos flexibles).

fact_refs.claim: 504 provides long-term, fixed-rate financing for major fixed assets (land, buildings, machinery, equipment) through CDCs working with private lenders.
Typical 504 structure: lender up to 50% of project cost, CDC up to 40%, borrower at least 10%; some projects require more (SBA.gov, as of Oct. 2026, subject to change).
504 loans cannot be used for working capital or inventory.
7(a) can fund working capital, changes of ownership, equipment, real estate and refinancing of certain business debt.

scripts.why_selected_es: Es la única pieza comparativa del lote y la única que cubre el 504. Ayuda a dueños con planes de crecimiento a elegir según el destino del dinero, y es una referencia práctica que se guarda.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: SBA loans explained] Objection: 'SBA loans take forever and need too much paperwork, so why bother?' An honest look at why the process is thorough.
scripts.audience: Owners and buyers weighing SBA financing against faster alternatives
scripts.problem: Some people skip SBA options because of how slow they seem, and others go in expecting speed. Both lead to bad planning.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amounts. Terms are SBA's typical maximum terms by use of proceeds (years). The provisional USD 300,000 figure is not used.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "'SBA loans take forever and need way too much paperwork.' Is that fair? Partly." | On-screen: "Why SBA loans need so much paperwork"
scripts.script:
"SBA loans take forever and need way too much paperwork." Is that fair? Partly. But there's a reason.

An SBA loan has two layers of requirements. First, the lender does its own credit analysis. Second, the lender has to document SBA's eligibility rules: business size, use of proceeds, whether you can get credit elsewhere on reasonable terms, and verifying your tax transcripts.

So yes, it's more paperwork. Why do people still consider it? One reason is term length. SBA's rule is the shortest appropriate term based on your ability to repay, typically ten years or less, and up to twenty-five years for real estate. That's as of October twenty twenty-six and can change.

I can't promise anyone a timeline. But organizing your documents early helps you plan.

What part of the paperwork worries you most? Reply and tell me.

Organizing documents early helps with planning (no timeline stated or implied).

scripts.topic: [Pillar: SBA loans explained] Q&A: 'Can I use an SBA loan for working capital to grow my business?' What that generally means and what lenders want to see.
scripts.audience: Current owners who need working capital or growth funding
scripts.problem: Owners think SBA loans are only for buying something, so they don't consider them for working capital or for financing growth.
scripts.amount_context: Five hundred thousand dollars is the SBA Express program cap, and five million dollars is the CAPLines line limit (SBA.gov, as of Oct. 2026). Neither is Kevin's deal size. The provisional USD 300,000 figure is not used.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "Can you use an SBA loan for working capital, not just to buy something?" | On-screen: "SBA loans for working capital?"
scripts.script:
Can you use an SBA loan for working capital, not just to buy something? Generally, yes.

Short- and long-term working capital is an eligible use of SBA seven-A loans. There are also seven-A options often used for it.

SBA Express goes up to five hundred thousand dollars and allows revolving lines. CAPLines is aimed at short-term and cyclical working-capital needs, with lines up to five million dollars. Those limits are as of October twenty twenty-six and subject to change.

Now, the part that matters most: what lenders look at. Under SBA's lending criteria, lenders consider your past earnings, your projected cash flow, and your ability to repay from the business. How much each one weighs depends on the lender.

If you're planning a working-capital request and have questions, send us a DM.

Hacer la pregunta inicial con curiosidad genuina y responder "Generally, yes" con un leve asentimiento. Ir más despacio en las cifras. Pausa antes de "what lenders look at" e inclinarse un poco hacia la cámara. CTA tranquilo, sin presión. Palabras totales: 131 (aprox. 54 s).

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying a franchise] What lenders look at when you finance a franchise: a 5-point checklist
scripts.audience: Aspiring franchise buyers before they apply
scripts.problem: Buyers concentrate on picking a brand and don't know what makes the lender comfortable with them as the borrower.
scripts.amount_context: No amounts used. No credit-score or liquidity minimums stated.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "Before a lender gets excited about your franchise brand, they look at you." | On-screen: "5 things lenders check before the brand"
scripts.script:
Before a lender gets excited about your franchise brand, they look at you. Here are five things most lenders check.

One: your credit history and character. How have you handled debt?

Two: management experience. Have you run a team, a location, or a business like this one?

Three: cash flow. Based on the projections, can the business realistically repay the loan?

Four: your own money in the deal, plus the cash you'll still have after closing.

Five: the brand itself. Lenders confirm the franchise is eligible, and many also review the franchise agreement and the FDD, which is the disclosure document the franchisor gives you.

And no, there's no single SBA-wide credit score cutoff. Lenders set their own, and how they weigh each point depends on the lender and your situation.

Save this before you apply. Questions about financing your business? Send us a DM.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying a franchise] Jargon explained: FDD Item 7, and why the total initial investment is much more than the franchise fee
scripts.audience: Aspiring franchise buyers comparing brands
scripts.problem: Buyers budget for the franchise fee and underestimate the full startup cost the lender will finance against.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amounts used. Item numbers (five, seven, nineteen, twenty-three) come from the FTC Franchise Rule.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "The franchise fee is not what it costs to open a franchise." | On-screen: "Franchise fee ≠ total cost. Read Item 7"
scripts.script:
The franchise fee is not what it costs to open a franchise. Here's the page that tells you the real number, and stay for item nineteen.

Every franchisor has to give you a disclosure document called the FDD. Under the current federal franchise rule, it has twenty-three items. Two matter a lot for financing.

Item five shows the initial fees you pay the franchisor before you open. That's the number most people anchor on.

Item seven is the estimated initial investment. It's a table that can include the fee plus real estate, equipment, build-out, opening inventory, deposits, licenses, and a line called additional funds, meaning money to keep the business running during an initial period.

That full range is what you plan around, not just the fee.

Item nineteen covers financial performance numbers, but franchisors don't have to provide them.

Save this for your FDD review.
scripts.cta: Save this for your FDD review.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying a franchise] Myth vs. fact: 'A big-name brand means the bank will fund me'
scripts.audience: Aspiring franchise buyers attracted to well-known brands
scripts.problem: Buyers expect brand recognition to get them through financing and skip preparing their own case.
scripts.amount_context: No amounts used. No failure or default statistics.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "'It's a big-name brand, so the bank will fund me.'" | On-screen: "MYTH: Big brand = loan approved"
scripts.script:
"It's a big-name brand, so the bank will fund me." It sounds logical, but it's a myth. Here's what's actually true.

SBA keeps a Franchise Directory. Lenders use it to check whether a brand is eligible for SBA financing. As of October twenty twenty-six, it's active and updated weekly.

But eligible doesn't mean approved. SBA says a listing is not an endorsement of the brand and doesn't ensure the business will succeed.

The lender still underwrites you: your credit history, your management experience, your cash flow projections, and the money you're putting in.

So a well-known brand may be part of the picture, but it doesn't replace your own preparation.

Know someone looking at a big franchise right now? Share this with them.

Word count: about 122 words, about 50 s at 148 wpm.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying a franchise] Hypothetical scenario: the buyer who forgets ramp-up working capital
scripts.audience: Aspiring franchise buyers in the planning stage
scripts.problem: Underestimating ramp-up working capital can leave a new franchise short of cash even when the loan closes.
scripts.amount_context: Hypothetical round number only: two hundred thousand dollars as the buyer's own budget for the fee plus build-out. Not typical costs. The USD 300,000 figure is not used.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "Here's how a franchise can close its loan and still run out of cash." | On-screen: "Loan closed. Cash gone. Why?" + "*Hypothetical, round numbers. Not typical costs."
scripts.script:
Here's how a franchise can close its loan and still run out of cash. This is a hypothetical example with round numbers, not typical costs.

A buyer budgets for the franchise fee and the build-out. Say that's two hundred thousand dollars total. The loan closes, and the doors open.

But in the first months, sales are still building, and rent, payroll and inventory are due every month anyway. Nobody planned for that gap.

That's the mistake: forgetting ramp-up cash. Two things can help.

First, look at item seven in the franchise disclosure document. It includes an additional funds estimate for an initial period of operation.

Second, working capital is an eligible use of SBA seven-A loans, which are made by lenders and partly guaranteed by the SBA. So it can be part of a franchise financing request, depending on lender underwriting.

Planning a franchise? Send us a DM with your questions.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying a franchise] Planning to open a franchise in the next 12 months? 3 questions to answer before you talk to a lender
scripts.audience: Franchise buyers who intend to move within 12 months (high intent)
scripts.problem: Serious buyers reach out to lenders without having the basic answers that make the first conversation useful.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amounts and no equity injection percentage (the start-up figure under SOP 50 10 8.1 is unconfirmed). The USD 300,000 figure is not used.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "Planning to open a franchise in the next twelve months?" | On-screen: "Franchise in the next 12 months? Answer these 3 first"
scripts.script:
Planning to open a franchise in the next twelve months? Answer these three questions before you talk to a lender.

One: how much of your own cash can you put in? Under current SBA rules, which can change, start-ups need an equity injection, meaning your own money in the deal, and lenders may require more. Know your number and where it comes from.

Two: what's the total investment, really? Not just the franchise fee. Look at item seven of the franchise disclosure document. It shows the franchisor's estimated initial investment range.

Three: what will your role be? Lenders consider who will manage the business day to day. Will that be you, or a manager you hire?

If you can answer all three, your first lender conversation can be much more productive.

Planning a franchise in the next year? Send us a DM.
scripts.cta: Planning a franchise in the next year? Send us a DM.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying an existing business] Jargon explained: what a seller note is, and how it can fit into an SBA acquisition deal alongside the bank loan and your cash.
scripts.audience: Acquisition buyers who are structuring their first offer
scripts.problem: Buyers hear 'seller financing' and either think it replaces the bank entirely or don't know it can be part of the deal at all.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amount used. Only the program percentage (ten percent minimum equity injection, per SOP 50 10 8.1 effective Oct. 1, 2026, subject to change). The USD 300,000 figure is not used.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "Seller financing doesn't replace the bank loan. In an SBA deal, it sits beside it." On-screen text: "Seller note ≠ no bank"
scripts.script:
Seller financing doesn't replace the bank loan. In an SBA deal, it sits beside it.

One: the bank loan, an SBA seven-a, a lender's loan partly guaranteed by the SBA.

Two: your cash.

Three: a seller note. That's a loan from the seller to you for part of the price, paid back over time instead of at closing.

Here's what most buyers miss. In a full buyout, under SBA rules effective October first, twenty twenty-six, a seller note can count toward the minimum ten percent equity injection, the money you bring in, only if it's on full standby. That means no payments to the seller for the life of the SBA loan.

And together with similar debt, it can cover no more than half of that injection. So no, it's not one hundred percent seller financing.

Subject to change. Save this before your first offer.
scripts.cta: Save this before your first offer.
scripts.structure: practical_explainer: numbered three-part breakdown, then an open loop ('Here's what most buyers miss') that pays off with the standby rule. About 146 spoken words, roughly 58–60 s at 145–150 wpm.
scripts.recording_notes_es: Plano medio, mirada a cámara. Tono calmado y didáctico. Marca 'uno, dos, tres' con los dedos. Haz una pausa breve antes de 'Here's what most buyers miss' e inclínate un poco hacia la cámara. Di 'full standby' más despacio y con énfasis. Termina con una sonrisa leve y sin prisa.
scripts.adaptation_note_es: De V06 solo tomamos el mecanismo de ajustar expectativas: la financiación del vendedor existe, pero tiene límites. No copiamos frases ni la estrategia de buscar operaciones con 100% de financiación del vendedor, porque esa idea queda fuera del contexto SBA. El guion está escrito desde cero.

fact_refs.claim: A seller note is a loan from the seller to the buyer for part of the purchase price, repaid over time instead of at closing.
SBA 7(a) loans are made by lenders and partly guaranteed by the SBA.
Under SOP 50 10 8.1 (effective Oct. 1, 2026), complete changes of ownership require at least a 10% equity injection; subject to change.
A seller note counts toward the equity injection only if it is on full standby (no principal or interest payments) for the life of the SBA loan.
Seller notes and other standby debt together can cover no more than half of the required injection, so an SBA deal is never 100% seller-financed.

scripts.why_selected_es: Es el único tema del lote sobre estructura de la operación. Corrige una confusión frecuente (que la financiación del vendedor sustituye al banco) y aporta una regla concreta que el comprador quiere tener a mano cuando prepara su oferta. Por eso el objetivo es que se guarde. RIESGO: las reglas de standby y del 50% vienen de resúmenes secundarios (bufete y consultora). El operador debe confirmarlas contra el Apéndice 15 del SOP 50 10 8.1 antes de publicar. No se insinúa respaldo de la SBA.
scripts.what_to_measure_es: Guardados por cada mil reproducciones, retención en el segundo 30 (después de 'Here's what most buyers miss'), porcentaje que ve el video completo y DMs cualificados sobre cómo estructurar ofertas. Las vistas no cuentan como leads.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying an existing business] Reality check: 'It's all about the business, not you.' In fact, lenders look at both the business's cash flow and the buyer.
scripts.audience: Acquisition buyers, especially first-timers without industry experience
scripts.problem: Popular content tells buyers that only the business matters, so they neglect their own resume, credit and liquidity.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amount used. Only the twenty percent ownership threshold for personal guaranties (SOP 50 10 8/8.1, as of Oct. 2026, subject to change). The USD 300,000 figure is not used.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "Reality check. You'll hear that buying a business is all about the business, not you." On-screen text: "Reality check: lenders look at YOU too"
scripts.script:
Reality check. You'll hear that buying a business is all about the business, not you. That's only half true.

Yes, lenders look hard at the business's cash flow and its ability to repay. But SBA lending criteria also include the buyer: your character and credit history, and your experience and depth of management. In plain English: can you actually run this?

And there's one more piece. Under SBA rules as of October twenty twenty-six, anyone who owns twenty percent or more generally has to sign a full, unlimited personal guaranty. That means you're personally on the hook if the loan isn't repaid. Lenders can ask others to guarantee too.

Rules can change, and every lender weighs this differently. So before you shop for a business, get your own resume, credit and cash story ready.

Send this to the partner you're buying with.
scripts.cta: Send this to the partner you're buying with.
scripts.structure: myth_vs_reality: 'Reality check' opener, then the myth, then the reveal ('only half true'), then the personal guaranty twist, then a share prompt. About 142 spoken words, roughly 57–60 s.
scripts.recording_notes_es: Abre con plano cerrado y energía firme en 'Reality check', con una pausa de medio segundo. Después pasa a un tono más conversacional. En 'can you actually run this?' levanta las cejas y haz una pausa. Di 'full, unlimited personal guaranty' despacio y con seriedad, sin dramatizar. En el CTA, gesto abierto con la mano hacia la cámara.
scripts.adaptation_note_es: De V01 solo usamos la estructura de apertura 'Reality check:' para interrumpir el scroll, y la usamos precisamente para corregir la afirmación del propio V01. No copiamos ni 'no banks, no hoops' ni ninguna otra frase, ni su tono exagerado.

fact_refs.claim: SBA lending criteria (13 CFR 120.150) include the business's cash flow and ability to repay, and the applicant's character, reputation, credit history, and experience and depth of management.
Under SOP 50 10 8 and 8.1 (as of Oct. 2026), owners of 20% or more generally must give a full, unlimited personal guaranty, and lenders may require guaranties from others; subject to change.
Each lender weighs these factors in its own credit analysis.

Funciona para compartir entre socios o con el cónyuge comprador, porque a los dos les afecta la garantía personal. RIESGO: la regla del 20% sale de un blog de un banco (fuente secundaria) y hay que confirmarla contra el SOP antes de publicar. No se promete aprobación y se insiste en que cada prestamista lo evalúa de forma distinta.
