scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying an existing business] Hypothetical walkthrough: DSCR (debt service coverage ratio) for buying a business, worked through with simple round numbers.
scripts.audience: Acquisition buyers looking at a listing's cash flow
scripts.problem: Buyers judge a deal by its asking price and its profit and don't check whether the cash flow can actually cover the loan payments.
scripts.amount_context: HYPOTHETICAL figures only: one hundred fifty thousand dollars of annual cash flow available for debt service and one hundred twenty thousand dollars of annual loan payments (DSCR 1.25x). These are not real deals and not the USD 300,000 figure.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "A business can show a profit and still not support the loan." On-screen text: "Profitable ≠ financeable"
scripts.script:
A business can show a profit and still not support the loan. The number that tells you is DSCR, debt service coverage ratio. Stay for the line lenders compare it to.

Here's the formula: cash flow available to pay debt, divided by your total annual loan payments, principal plus interest.

Hypothetical, round numbers. The business produces one hundred fifty thousand dollars a year available for debt. Your loan payments total one hundred twenty thousand a year. One fifty divided by one twenty is one point two five. So, a dollar twenty-five of cash flow for every dollar of payments.

Now the line. The SBA sets a minimum, and many lenders want more. Under rules effective October first, twenty twenty-six, most business purchases need at least one point two five, based on past cash flow, not projections.

Subject to change. Save this for your next listing.
scripts.cta: Save this for your next listing.
scripts.structure: scenario: open loop ('Stay for the line lenders compare it to'), then the formula, then a hypothetical worked example, then the loop pays off with the SBA minimum. About 145 spoken words, roughly 58–60 s.
scripts.recording_notes_es: Plano medio, ritmo pausado y claro. Al decir los números, haz una pausa breve entre cada uno para que se puedan seguir. Puedes marcar la división con un gesto de una mano encima de la otra. Di 'Hypothetical' con énfasis claro. Antes de 'Now the line' haz una pausa y mira directo a cámara para cerrar el bucle abierto.
scripts.adaptation_note_es: De V07 solo tomamos la estructura de ejemplo resuelto con números redondos: analogía, fórmula y cálculo. No usamos el concepto inmobiliario de 'DSCR loan', ni la idea de que el DSCR basta para aprobar, ni la automatización por palabra clave. Las cifras están adaptadas a la compra de un negocio y etiquetadas como hipotéticas.

fact_refs.claim: DSCR = cash flow available for debt service ÷ total annual debt payments (principal plus interest); 1.25x means $1.25 of cash flow per $1.00 of payments.
Hypothetical example: $150,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.25x (arithmetic checked; labeled hypothetical in speech).
SBA sets a minimum DSCR and many lenders require more.

Under SOP 50 10 8.1 (effective Oct. 1, 2026), most change-of-ownership loans need at least 1.25x, measured on historical cash flow, and projections generally can't make up for a shortfall; subject to change.

scripts.why_selected_es: Es el único tema del lote con un cálculo. El ejemplo numérico y el bucle abierto ayudan a mantener la atención hasta el final, y enseña a filtrar anuncios de venta por algo más que su precio. RIESGO: el mínimo de 1,25x viene de un bufete y de fuentes secundarias, así que hay que verificarlo contra el SOP 50 10 8.1. El ejemplo es hipotético y no menciona aprobación.
scripts.what_to_measure_es: Retención media, porcentaje que llega al final (pago del bucle abierto), repeticiones, guardados y DMs cualificados de compradores que tienen un anuncio concreto. Las vistas no son leads.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying an existing business] Asking price vs. what a lender will finance: why the listing price isn't automatically the number the deal gets funded on.
scripts.audience: Acquisition buyers about to make an offer
scripts.problem: Buyers anchor on the seller's asking price and get caught out when the valuation or the cash flow doesn't support it.
scripts.amount_context: Only the program threshold of three million dollars purchase price for a quality of earnings review (SOP 50 10 8.1, Oct. 1, 2026, subject to change). The USD 300,000 figure is not used.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "The asking price is the seller's number. The lender works from a different one." On-screen text: "Asking price vs. what gets financed"
scripts.script:
The asking price is the seller's number. The lender works from a different one. Here's how they compare, in three checks.

Check one: valuation. Under SBA rules effective October first, twenty twenty-six, every change of ownership needs an independent business valuation. And the SBA loan is generally limited to that value, so goodwill, the value beyond the physical assets, has to be supported by it.

Check two: verified numbers. Lenders compare the seller's financials to IRS tax transcripts. And add-backs, the expenses the seller says shouldn't count against profit, must be documented and can be adjusted or rejected.

Check three: bigger deals. If an acquisition's purchase price is three million dollars or more, a quality of earnings review, a deeper accounting check, is also required.

Subject to change. If the price isn't supported, that gap needs a plan before you sign.

Planning an offer? Send us a DM.
scripts.cta: Planning an offer? Send us a DM.
scripts.structure: comparison: asking price vs. lender's number, structured as a numbered list of three checks, ending with a takeaway and a soft DM CTA. About 146 spoken words, roughly 58–60 s.
scripts.recording_notes_es: Plano medio. En la primera frase, haz un gesto de 'dos números' con una mano a cada lado. Cuenta 'check one, two, three' con los dedos. Tono seguro y sin alarmismo. Haz una pausa antes de 'If the price isn't supported' y baja un poco el ritmo. En el CTA, tono cálido e invitación tranquila.
scripts.adaptation_note_es: Original: no se basa en ninguna referencia. Mecanismo propio de comparación en tres chequeos.

fact_refs.claim: Under SOP 50 10 8.1 (effective Oct. 1, 2026), the prior $250,000 lender-valuation exception no longer appears, so every change of ownership requires an independent qualified valuation; subject to change.
Goodwill and intangible value must be supported by the valuation, and the SBA change-of-ownership loan is generally capped at the valuation amount.
Lenders verify seller financials against IRS tax transcripts; add-backs must be documented and may be adjusted or rejected.
A quality of earnings report is required for initial acquisitions (and business expansions) with a purchase price of $3 million or more under SOP 50 10 8.1.

scripts.why_selected_es: Es el único tema sobre valoración. Ataca el anclaje en el precio pedido justo antes de que el comprador haga su oferta, que es un momento de alta intención, y por eso cierra con un CTA de consulta por DM. RIESGO: la valoración obligatoria, el tope de goodwill y el umbral del QoE vienen de una firma de valoración (fuente secundaria) y deben confirmarse contra el SOP. Las definiciones de 'goodwill' y 'add-backs' son explicaciones en lenguaje sencillo. No se promete financiación.
scripts.what_to_measure_es: Retención en cada uno de los tres chequeos, porcentaje que ve el video completo, guardados y DMs cualificados de compradores que tienen una oferta en preparación. Las vistas no son leads.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Buying an existing business] Planning to buy a business in the next 12 months? Know these 3 numbers: how much cash you can inject, the business's verified cash flow, and the estimated annual loan payments.
scripts.audience: Acquisition buyers who intend to buy within 12 months (high intent)
scripts.problem: Motivated buyers start browsing listings without knowing the three numbers that decide whether a deal is financeable at all.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amount used. Only the ten percent minimum equity injection (SOP 50 10 8.1, as of Oct. 2026, subject to change) and a three-year review window. The USD 300,000 figure is not used.
scripts.hook: Spoken: "Planning to buy a business in the next twelve months? Before you scroll another listing, know these three numbers." On-screen text: "Buying in the next 12 months? Know these 3 numbers"
scripts.script:
Planning to buy a business in the next twelve months? Before you scroll another listing, know these three numbers.

Number one: your cash injection, the money you put into the deal. Under SBA rules as of October twenty twenty-six, a complete change of ownership needs at least ten percent of total project costs, and lenders can require more.

Number two: the business's verified cash flow. Not the listing's number. Lenders review tax returns and financial statements, usually the last three years, and check them against IRS transcripts.

Number three: your estimated annual loan payments. Because the real question is whether that verified cash flow can cover them, with room to spare.

These rules can change. If one of these numbers is still blank, that's normal. It's where planning starts.

Buying in the next year? Send us a DM and tell us which number you're stuck on.
scripts.cta: Buying in the next year? Send us a DM and tell us which number you're stuck on.
scripts.structure: question: intent-qualifying question as the hook, then a numbered list of three numbers, then a reassurance, then a DM CTA with a specific prompt. About 147 spoken words, roughly 59–60 s.
scripts.recording_notes_es: Plano cerrado al principio, haz la pregunta mirando directo a cámara y con calma. Levanta un dedo por cada número. En 'Not the listing's number' haz un pequeño gesto de negación con la cabeza. En 'that's normal' usa un tono tranquilizador y cálido. Termina en silencio un segundo, mirando a cámara.
scripts.adaptation_note_es: De V05 solo tomamos el enfoque de hablarle directamente a compradores de adquisiciones que buscan un préstamo SBA. Descartamos la afirmación de que los préstamos pequeños son difíciles de conseguir porque es una opinión del creador y no está verificada. No copiamos ninguna frase.

fact_refs.claim: Under SOP 50 10 8.1 (Oct. 1, 2026), as under SOP 50 10 8, complete changes of ownership require an equity injection of at least 10% of total project costs; lenders may require more; subject to change.
Lenders review business tax returns and financial statements, typically for the most recent three years, and verify them against IRS transcripts.
Lenders assess whether business cash flow can repay the debt (repayment ability).

scripts.why_selected_es: Es el tema de mayor intención del bloque de adquisiciones. La pregunta inicial filtra a quienes compran en los próximos 12 meses, y el CTA pide un dato concreto, lo que favorece conversaciones cualificadas por DM. RIESGO: el 10% viene de fuentes de bufete y consultora y debe confirmarse contra el SOP. No se promete aprobación y se descartó lo no verificado de V05.
scripts.what_to_measure_es: DMs cualificados (que mencionen un plazo de compra o uno de los tres números), visitas al perfil, veces compartido y guardados. También la retención hasta el número tres. Las vistas no son leads.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Getting loan ready] Checklist: documents lenders commonly ask for in a business loan request
scripts.audience: All three groups: franchise buyers, acquisition buyers and owners seeking capital
scripts.problem: Applicants gather documents piece by piece as they're asked for them, which drags out the process and makes them look unprepared.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amount used.
scripts.hook: SPOKEN (0–3 s): "If you're planning a business loan request, here's a checklist worth saving before a lender asks." | ON-SCREEN: "5 documents to gather BEFORE the lender asks"
scripts.script: If you're planning a business loan request, here's a checklist worth saving before a lender asks. Number one: business and personal tax returns. Generally, it's the last three years, and lenders usually check them against IRS transcripts. Number two: a personal financial statement. For SBA seven A loans, that's SBA Form four thirteen. It lays out what you own and what you owe. Number three: the borrower information form, SBA Form nineteen nineteen. It covers you, your owners and your existing debts, so have a list of current business debts ready. Number four: a short resume. Lenders look at management experience. Number five: projections or a business plan, because lenders consider projected cash flow. And keep in mind, each lender may ask for more than this. Save this checklist, and if you have questions about financing your business, send us a DM.
scripts.cta: Save this checklist, and if you have questions about financing your business, send us a DM.
scripts.structure:
checklist — Hook (0–3 s) → #1 Tax returns (3–12 s; on-screen: "Business + personal tax returns / generally last 3 years") → #2 SBA Form 413 (12–21 s; "Personal Financial Statement (SBA Form 413)") → #3 SBA Form 1919 + debt list (21–31 s; "Borrower Information Form (SBA Form 1919) + list of current debts") → #4 Resume (31–36 s; "Short resume: management experience") → #5 Projections/plan (36–42 s; "Projections or business plan") → Payoff: lenders may ask for more (42–46 s; "Each lender may ask for more" / "*Form versions as of Oct 2026, subject to change") → CTA (46–55 s). Retention device: numbered list (1–5) with a running counter. Est. 142 words ≈ 57–60 s at 140–150 wpm. Designer: #0B2545 background, #F4F6F8 Inter captions, #E0A526 numbered counter in the top-right safe zone, checklist ticks animate on each item; captions stay inside the 4:5 safe zone. Caption: "Gathering documents one request at a time slows everything down.
Here are 5 items lenders commonly ask for in a business loan request. Save it for later.
Each lender may ask for more, so confirm with yours.
This content is for educational purposes only and is not financial, legal or tax advice. Loan programs, terms and eligibility are subject to change and lender approval." Hashtags: #SBALoan #SmallBusinessFunding #BusinessLoan #LoanReady #BusinessFinancing. Risk note: the form names and versions (Form 1919 effective Mar 19, 2025; Form 413 effective Feb 13, 2025) are only partially verified and could be revised after the 2026 citizenship changes, so recheck SBA.gov before publishing. The resume and projections items are framed as preparation linked to lender criteria, not as SBA-mandated forms. No promise of speed or approval.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Getting loan ready] Jargon explained: equity injection — what it is, why lenders want skin in the game, and how its source is documented
scripts.audience: Franchise and acquisition buyers planning their down payment
scripts.problem: Buyers don't know that lenders scrutinize where the cash comes from, and they may be planning to use sources that don't qualify.
scripts.amount_context: Ten percent minimum equity injection for complete changes of ownership (SOP 50 10 8.1, effective Oct 1, 2026). No dollar amount used.
scripts.hook: SPOKEN (0–3 s): "Equity injection is simple: it's the money you put into the deal yourself." | ON-SCREEN: "Equity injection, explained in 45 seconds"
scripts.script: Equity injection is simple: it's the money you put into the deal yourself. Think of it as skin in the game. Here's the part many buyers miss. It's not just how much you bring, it's whether you can prove where it came from. Under current SBA rules, as of October twenty twenty-six, the minimum for a complete change of ownership is ten percent of total project costs, and that's subject to change. Commonly cited sources include cash or savings, and documented gifts that don't have to be repaid. In limited cases, a seller note can cover part of it, generally only if the seller takes no payments for the life of the loan, and capped at half of the required injection. Lenders must verify the source, so expect to show bank statements, wire records or a gift letter. Save this before you plan your down payment.
scripts.cta: Save this before you plan your down payment.

practical_explainer — Hook/definition (0–4 s; on-screen: "Equity injection = your own money in the deal") → Skin in the game (4–6 s) → Open loop: 'the part many buyers miss' (6–14 s; "It's not just HOW MUCH. It's WHERE it came from.") → Rule (14–26 s; "Min. 10% for complete changes of ownership" / "*SOP 50 10 8.1, as of Oct 1, 2026. Subject to change") → Sources (26–32 s; "Commonly cited: cash/savings, documented gifts") → Seller note (32–44 s; "Seller note: only on full standby, max ½ of required injection" / "*Confirm with your lender") → Documentation (44–52 s; "Bank statements · wire records · gift letter") → CTA (52–56 s). Retention device: open loop ('the part many buyers miss') plus a reveal. Est. 145 words ≈ 58–60 s. Designer: #13315C background, key term in an #E0A526 highlight box, Inter bold, simple icons for document types, all text inside the safe zone. Caption: "Equity injection is your own contribution to the deal.
Lenders look at the amount and also at whether you can document where it came from.
Save this before you plan your down payment.
This content is for educational purposes only and is not financial, legal or tax advice. Loan programs, terms and eligibility are subject to change and lender approval." scripts.topic: [Pillar: Getting loan ready] Objection: 'My credit is good, so why do I need projections and a business plan?'
scripts.audience: Owners seeking growth capital and first-time buyers with strong personal credit
scripts.problem: Applicants rely on a good credit score and arrive without a credible repayment story.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amount used.
scripts.hook: SPOKEN (0–3 s): "My credit score is excellent, so why does the lender want projections and a plan?" | ON-SCREEN: "Great credit… so why do lenders want projections?"
scripts.script: My credit score is excellent, so why does the lender want projections and a plan? It's a fair question. Credit is one factor, but it's not the whole picture. For SBA loans, lenders have to look at your credit history and at whether the business can repay the loan from its earnings and cash flow. Your score shows how you've handled debt in the past. It doesn't show whether this business can cover this new payment. That's your repayment story. If you're starting something new, many lenders ask for projections or a business plan, because there's no history yet. If you're buying an existing business, historical cash flow generally carries the most weight, and projections usually can't cover a shortfall. So good credit helps. The repayment story matters just as much. Have questions about financing your business? Send us a DM.
scripts.cta: Have questions about financing your business? Send us a DM.

objection — Hook: objection voiced (0–4 s) → Reframe (4–9 s; "Credit = one factor") → Rule (9–20 s; "SBA lenders weigh: credit history + ability to repay from business cash flow") → Contrast (20–29 s; "Your score = the past. Cash flow = this payment.") → Start-up vs acquisition split (29–48 s; "Start-up: projections / business plan" | "Acquisition: historical cash flow weighs most" / "*In general; depends on lender and deal") → Payoff (48–53 s; "Credit helps. Repayment story matters just as much.") → CTA (53–58 s). Retention device: objection followed by a reveal and a start-up vs. acquisition contrast. Est. 142 words ≈ 57–60 s. Designer: split screen for the contrast (left #0B2545 'Credit score', right #13315C 'Cash flow'), #E0A526 underline on 'repayment story', Inter, captions inside the safe zone. Caption: "Good credit is a strong start, but it's one factor among several.
For SBA loans, lenders also look at whether the business can repay from its own cash flow.
What's your repayment story?
This content is for educational purposes only and is not financial, legal or tax advice. Loan programs, terms and eligibility are subject to change and lender approval." Hashtags: #SBALoan #SmallBusinessOwner #BusinessLoan #CashFlow #LoanReady. Risk note: SBSS/FICO scores are deliberately left out per research. This is not credit repair content. The point that projections can't cover a shortfall applies to acquisitions under SOP 50 10 8.1 and comes from a law-firm summary, so it's hedged with 'generally' and 'usually'. No suggestion that good credit leads to approval.
scripts.recording_notes_es: Abre con la objeción en tono de cliente (curioso, con un leve gesto de encogerse de hombros). Después cambia a tu tono consultivo y mira de frente al lente. Usa las manos para el contraste: una mano 'el pasado', la otra 'este pago'. Pausa antes de 'That's your repayment story.' Cierre firme y calmado.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Getting loan ready] Top 5 mistakes that can slow down or weaken a business loan request
scripts.audience: All groups, particularly owners preparing their first loan request
scripts.problem: Avoidable issues create back-and-forth with the lender and make the borrower look less credible.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amount used.
scripts.hook: SPOKEN (0–3 s): "Five mistakes that can slow down a business loan request, and they're avoidable." | ON-SCREEN: "5 avoidable mistakes in a loan request"
scripts.script: Five mistakes that can slow down a business loan request, and they're avoidable. One: mixing personal and business money in the same account. It makes your numbers harder for a lender to follow. Two: tax returns that are missing or don't match your financials. Lenders generally check your numbers against IRS transcripts, and discrepancies have to be resolved. Three: a down payment you can't document. Lenders need to see where your equity injection, meaning your own money in the deal, came from and that it went into the deal, usually through bank statements and transfer records. Four: numbers that don't line up across your documents. Every gap becomes a question. Five: no clear use of funds. If you can't say exactly what the money is for, it's hard for a lender to evaluate. Know someone getting ready to apply? Share this with them.
scripts.cta: Know someone getting ready to apply? Share this with them.
scripts.structure:
checklist (mistakes) — Hook (0–3 s) → #1 Commingling (3–10 s; "Mixing personal + business money") → #2 Tax returns (10–20 s; "Missing or mismatched tax returns" / "*Lenders generally verify via IRS transcripts") → #3 Undocumented down payment (20–35 s; "Down payment you can't document" / "Equity injection = your own money in the deal") → #4 Inconsistent numbers (35–41 s; "Numbers that don't match") → #5 No use of funds (41–50 s; "No clear use of funds") → CTA (50–57 s). Retention device: numbered countdown with an ✕ mark on each mistake. Est. 145 words ≈ 58–60 s. Designer: #0B2545 background, red-free palette (use an #E0A526 ✕), Inter bold headlines, counter '1/5…5/5' in the safe zone, light #F4F6F8 caption bar. Caption: "These are general patterns, not statistics, but each one can create extra back-and-forth with a lender.
Which of the 5 is easiest to fix today?
Share this with someone preparing a loan request.
This content is for educational purposes only and is not financial, legal or tax advice. Loan programs, terms and eligibility are subject to change and lender approval." Hashtags: #BusinessLoan #SmallBusinessTips #SBALoan #LoanReady #BuyABusiness. Risk note: no statistics are used. Mistakes 1, 4 and 5 are general preparation guidance with no program rule behind them, so they're phrased as practical observations. Says 'can slow down', never promises faster processing. Form 4506-C/8821 details are left out of the spoken text because they are only partially verified.

scripts.topic: [Pillar: Getting loan ready] Not every lender wants every deal: why lender fit matters before you apply
scripts.audience: Buyers and owners who are getting ready to approach lenders
scripts.problem: Applicants treat lenders as interchangeable, then read a 'no' as a dead end when the real problem may simply have been the wrong fit.
scripts.amount_context: No dollar amount used.
scripts.hook: SPOKEN (0–3 s): "Here's something many first-time borrowers don't realize: a no from one lender isn't always a no on your deal." | ON-SCREEN: "One lender said no. Is your deal dead?"
scripts.script: Here's something many first-time borrowers don't realize: a no from one lender isn't always a no on your deal. Sometimes it's just the wrong fit. Lenders differ in the loan sizes, industries and deal types they focus on. Each lender decides which deal sizes fit its business, and they set their own credit policies within SBA rules. There's another layer with SBA loans. SBA gives delegated authority only to qualified lenders, called preferred lenders. They can generally approve most loans without SBA reviewing them first. Other lenders generally go through that SBA review. So before you apply, it's worth asking a few questions. Do you finance deals this size? Do you work with my industry? Do you do acquisitions or franchise loans? Fit doesn't guarantee approval, but it can save you from knocking on the wrong door. Planning a purchase or a funding request? Send us a DM.
scripts.cta: Planning a purchase or a funding request? Send us a DM.
scripts.structure:
direct_statement — Counter-intuitive hook (0–5 s) → Reframe: wrong fit (5–7 s) → Why: lenders differ (7–20 s; "Lenders differ by: loan size · industry · deal type") → Insider layer: PLP (20–35 s; "Preferred lenders (PLP): delegated authority" / "*Only qualified lenders; SBA rules still apply") → 3 questions to ask (35–47 s; "Ask: deal size? industry? acquisitions/franchise?") → Payoff + hedge (47–53 s; "Fit ≠ approval") → CTA (53–58 s). Retention device: counter-intuitive statement as an open loop, then 3 practical questions. Est. 145 words ≈ 58–60 s. Designer: #0B2545 background, three 'door' cards in #13315C with an #E0A526 highlight on the matching door, Inter, captions inside the safe zone. Caption: "Lenders aren't interchangeable. They differ in the loan sizes, industries and deal types they focus on.
Ask about fit before you apply.
Planning a purchase or a funding request? Send us a DM.
This content is for educational purposes only and is not financial, legal or tax advice. Loan programs, terms and eligibility are subject to change and lender approval." Hashtags: #SBALoan #BuyABusiness #FranchiseFinancing #BusinessLoan #SmallBusinessFunding. Risk note: V05's claim that small loans are harder to place was not verified and is left out. It is reframed neutrally as 'each lender decides which deal sizes fit its business'. No lender partnerships or relationships are implied for Livetrust. The script says plainly that fit doesn't guarantee approval.
scripts.recording_notes_es: Abre con tono de confidencia, como compartiendo algo que pocos saben; mirada directa y una pausa de medio segundo después de 'isn't always a no on your deal'. Ritmo calmado en la parte de lenders preferidos. Cuenta las tres preguntas con los dedos. Cierre cálido y consultivo, sin vender.
scripts.adaptation_note_es: De V05 (@owneractions) solo se adapta la mecánica: una verdad contraintuitiva del lado del prestamista, luego la razón desde su perspectiva y después el contexto. No se copian frases ni se usa su afirmación no verificada (que los préstamos SBA pequeños son más difíciles de conseguir); se reemplaza por la formulación neutral verificada.
